summary: Weekly POC check-in focused on reducing first-token and streaming tail latencies by using kernel hedging and tuned sequence-length profiles. Decided on two canary seqlen runs and Redwood to deliver a concise kernel hedging recommendation plus a config template. Security/KMS follow-up for private pilot remains blocked until Marco confirms access.
transcript:
[00:00] Lena Park: Okay good morning everyone, thanks for joining. Agenda — quick recap of last week's microbenchmarks, kernel hedging proposal, canary plan, and blockers. Emma, you had wanted to open?
[00:22] Emma Liu: Yeah thanks Lena. Quick note — Raj ran the broad set of prompts against our baseline and we still see p50 TTFT around 110ms but p95/p99 spikes, particularly for streaming contexts when responses are longer. Looks like some sequences cut through a different codepath.
[00:38] Raj Patel: Yeah I threw in a couple longer-history chat tests; the KV cache warmup is ok but the streaming handshake seems to add extra jitter. Also saw a handful of 800ms outliers when seq length hit ~700 tokens.
[00:55] Ethan Brooks: Got it. So two main things — short first token (TTFT) variance and larger multi-token streaming tails. Our idea is kernel hedging: try a faster, lower-precision kernel for the first few tokens and automatically switch to a robust kernel once we detect heavy attention/sequence costs. That should keep median TTFT down while bounding tail.
[01:20] Marco Ruiz: When you say "switch", is that a cold model reload? We can't afford that on the private pilot.
[01:30] Ethan Brooks: No. It's in-runtime kernel selection, not swapping weights. The runtime can pick different kernels or codepaths per layer or per block size. There's some overhead but usually sub-ms; we hedge by running the fast kernel path and if certain heuristics trigger, move to the robust kernel for remaining tokens.
[01:48] Sophie Tan: Sorry, quick clarifying — this is different from quantization profile change?
[01:54] Ethan Brooks: Yes related but distinct. Quantization is on-model weights; hedging chooses different execution kernels with different numeric stability / throughput tradeoffs. You can think of it as selecting fast-gemm variant vs. stable-gemm variant.
[02:08] Emma Liu: Cool. Do you have any numbers from your infra bench?
[02:12] Ethan Brooks: We ran a small internal bench on 2xA800 with the 13B model and saw TTFT median go from 95ms down to 70ms with the hedged first-token policy, and p99 improved as well because the fallback avoids catastrophic slow kernels. But of course your seqlen distribution matters a lot.
[02:33] Raj Patel: Our observed distribution — we have a long tail, about 12% of requests exceed 300 tokens, maybe 4% exceed 600. If we drop to a fixed 128 seqlen we lose context. Can hedging help for mixed seqlen?
[02:49] Ethan Brooks: Yes — that's the point of profile-aware hedging. We can use request headers or a lightweight per-request seqlen estimator to pick an initial policy. For example, if you often go beyond 512 we lean more conservative after a few tokens.
[03:05] Marco Ruiz: Does this interact with KV cache eviction? I'm worried about memory thrash.
[03:10] Ethan Brooks: Good call. Hedging keeps the same KV layout; we don't re-allocate caches on switch. But if you change chunking or block sizes, there may be transient increases in memory. We can configure margin limits.
[03:23] Lena Park: Quick administrative — I uploaded the benchmark slices sheet to the shared drive (link in calendar). Ethan, can you speak to recommended canary runs?
[03:33] Ethan Brooks: Sure. We recommend two controlled canaries: 1) seqlen-128 heavy short-turn dataset to validate TTFT wins and streaming start handshake; 2) seqlen-256/512 mixed to validate hedging doesn't regress p99 for long responses. Keep 5k requests each, capture p50/p95/p99, cold vs warm starts, and full trace including kernel-choice tags.
[03:55] Raj Patel: 5k sounds reasonable. We can do that on our dev infra overnight. Note: our dev GPUs are older-ish, call them T4-equivalents; results will be slower but comparative trends ok?
[04:07] Ethan Brooks: Yes, perfect. Please annotate hardware in the spreadsheet. We'll then map to what we expect on Redwood dedicated vs your private setup.
[04:18] Marco Ruiz: On security — I still don't have KMS linked for the private pilot. That blocks rolling out any private config; we need a KMS policy from Redwood.
[04:28] Lena Park: Sorry about that, Maya is looped on the thread — Maya, can you confirm the KMS policy template?
[04:34] Maya Ortiz: Yep I'll drop the template and the minimal steps. Marco, we need the IAM role id and a service account; I have a short checklist.
[04:42] Marco Ruiz: I can get that by Monday.
[04:45] Emma Liu: Back to hedging — is there risk of quality variance? We can't have hallucination regressions while improving TTFT.
[04:52] Ethan Brooks: Absolutely valid. We'll couple hedging thresholds with a lightweight eval set to watch for generation quality regressions. For the canaries we'll run sampling at low temperature to compare token overlap and a few automated scores plus human spot-checks on a 50-example set.
[05:08] Raj Patel: Ok. Also curious about streaming buffer sizes — do you recommend small chunking for low-latency or larger chunks for throughput?
[05:16] Ethan Brooks: For your use case, smaller initial chunks (e.g., 16 tokens) reduce first-byte delay but can increase overhead. Our hedging recommendation: start with 8-16 token chunks for the initial streaming handshake, then switch to larger chunks (32-64) once the model moves into steady-state. That reduces TTFT and overall token cost.
[05:36] Sophie Tan: Are those chunking changes in the SDK or runtime?
[05:39] Ethan Brooks: Runtime option with SDK hinting. The SDK can pass preferred chunk size and hedging policy; runtime enforces safe limits.
[05:46] Emma Liu: Any special config for sequence trimming? We have many user messages that are long but could be truncated smartly.
[05:53] Ethan Brooks: Yes — recommend heuristic trimming: keep last N tokens of user context plus a compressed summary of earlier history. We've got a small plugin that generates a 40–80 token summary which often preserves quality and reduces seqlen for many sessions. We can demo that next week.
[06:10] Raj Patel: Nice. For the canaries, should we include the summary plugin? Might bias results.
[06:15] Ethan Brooks: Start without the plugin so we baseline. Then run a second pass with summary to show marginal gains.
[06:21] Lena Park: Great. Any vendor comparisons we should call out?
[06:25] Emma Liu: We briefly considered Lambda Labs for lower-cost infra, but the managed infra and hedging features are the reason we're talking to Redwood. Also internal self-host is an option but we want to avoid long infra ops.
[06:36] Marco Ruiz: One practical question — if hedging triggers more robust kernels mid-request, do we pay extra compute?
[06:43] Ethan Brooks: Minimal. The runtime may switch to a heavier kernel which costs slightly more per token, but hedging is designed so the fallback only happens on a small percentage of requests. On average cost delta is small and often offset by reduced retries and better SLA compliance.
[06:58] Sophie Tan: Timeline — can we get the kernel doc and config by next Monday?
[07:02] Ethan Brooks: Yes — I'll put together a 2-page doc, a sample JSON config showing hedging thresholds, and a short troubleshooting checklist.
[07:10] Lena Park: And I will put pricing snapshot with dedicated burst options.
[07:14] Emma Liu: For the canary runs: we also want sample traces with the kernel-choice tag so we can see which kernel executed per token.
[07:21] Raj Patel: I'll add the logging flag in our harness.
[07:24] Ethan Brooks: Note: in streaming scenarios kernel tags may be slightly off in the ASR transcript — the tag is per block not per token in our current trace format.
[07:33] Raj Patel: fine as long as we can correlate.
[07:36] Emma Liu: Any blockers besides KMS?
[07:38] Marco Ruiz: Network egress rules in our VPC — we need a static egress IP or VPC peering to Redwood control plane for telemetry. I opened a ticket but haven't heard back.
[07:50] Lena Park: I have a contact with our infra team to expedite peering — I'll follow up with Marco after the call.
[07:56] Sophie Tan: For success criteria — remind me what we decided?
[07:59] Lena Park: Quick recap: target TTFT median <90ms on comparable infra or improvement of at least 20% from baseline, p99 < 500ms on streaming traces for 95% of traffic, and no measurable generation quality regressions on the eval set.
[08:15] Emma Liu: Sounds good.
[08:17] Lena Park: Ok final — schedule follow-up 30m early next week, same time Thursday? I can do Wed as well.
[08:24] Emma Liu: Thursday works.
[08:26] Lena Park: Great. Thanks everyone. I'll drop notes and the action items.
[08:30] -- end of recording --

Notes on transcription quality: occasional mis-hearings ("K V cash" for K V cache, "hedged" sometimes transcribed as "edged"). Some speaker labels merged (Emma/Emma Liu interchanged). Links referenced: benchmark-slices.xlsx (shared drive), kernel-hedging-draft.pdf (to be shared).
